en: To become less intense or widespread; to decrease
hook: ABATE: the storm takes A BATH and calms down.
story: Abate. All night, Cyclone Sitrang screamed over the coast of Bhola. Tin roofs flew like paper. Palm trees bent to the ground. Families huddled in the concrete shelter, children crying, nobody sleeping. Then, around dawn, the howling slowly softened. By nine, only a steady breeze remained. By noon, birds were singing again. The storm had abated: it had become less intense, little by little. Pain abates, anger abates, floods abate. Think of a storm taking a long, calming bath.

gre.s: The protesters vowed to continue until the government met their demands, so their anger is unlikely to ____ any time soon.
gre.clue: vowed to continue until the government met their demands

example: Once the fever began to abate, Nadia's grandmother finally allowed her to sit up in bed and read.

en: To give extra support to an argument or structure
hook: BUTTRESS: the stone supports holding up a cathedral wall.
story: Buttress. The old mosque in Farhan's town had a cracked wall that leaned a little more each monsoon. Engineers built thick brick supports against it from the outside, and the wall stopped moving. Those supports are called buttresses. As a verb, to buttress is to support or strengthen, and it is often used for arguments: Sara buttressed her thesis with data from forty villages. Gothic cathedrals in Europe are famous for their flying buttresses. Synonyms: bolster, reinforce, shore up.

gre.s: Knowing that the jury would distrust a single witness, the lawyer sought to ____ her argument with testimony from three independent experts.
gre.clue: Knowing that the jury would distrust a single witness

example: The researchers buttressed their claim about river pollution with water samples taken from twelve sites along the Buriganga.

en: Causing sudden, violent, and widespread destruction or change
hook: CATACLYSMIC: a CATastrophe, a total CRASH.
story: Cataclysmic. On the night of 12 November 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck the coast of what is now Bangladesh. A wall of seawater several metres high swept across the islands in the darkness. By morning, hundreds of thousands of people had died, and entire villages had vanished. It remains one of the deadliest natural disasters in history. It was cataclysmic: causing sudden, violent, widespread destruction. A cataclysm changes everything that follows.

gre.s: Geologists believe that a ____ asteroid impact, which triggered firestorms and years of darkness, wiped out the dinosaurs.
gre.clue: which triggered firestorms and years of darkness

example: Sailors hundreds of miles away heard the cataclysmic eruption of Krakatoa in 1883, which tore the island apart and cooled global weather.

en: To surprise or confuse someone, especially by contradicting expectations
hook: CONFOUND: CONFUSED and DUMBFOUNDED.
story: Confound. Everyone in the village said Ruksana could never pass the board exams: her family was poor, she had no tutor, and she studied by kerosene lamp. When the results came, she had the highest marks in the district. She confounded all their predictions: she surprised and confused people by contradicting what they expected. Confound can also mean to mix up, as in confounding two similar words. It comes from Latin for pouring together, everything mixed into confusion.

gre.s: The candidate's landslide victory managed to ____ the pollsters, who had confidently predicted for months that she would lose by a wide margin.
gre.clue: who had confidently predicted for months that she would lose by a wide margin

example: The patient's swift recovery confounded her doctors, who had warned the family to expect several months in hospital.

en: To expose a claim or belief as false
bn: মিথ্যা প্রমাণ করা; ভুল ধরিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: DE-BUNK: removes the BUNK (nonsense).
story: Debunk. One morning a viral post spread across every family WhatsApp group: drinking hot water every hour kills dangerous viruses. Aunties forwarded it. Uncles shared it. Within a day, doctors and fact-checkers debunked it, showing clearly that the claim had no scientific basis at all. To debunk is to expose a claim or belief as false. Think: de-bunk, removing the bunk, which is nonsense. Scientists spend a lot of time debunking popular myths.

gre.s: The documentary set out to ____ the popular myth that the ancient monument was built by a lost civilization, presenting overwhelming evidence of its ordinary origins.
gre.clue: presenting overwhelming evidence of its ordinary origins

example: In her first lecture, the physics teacher debunked the idea that heavier objects always fall faster than lighter ones.

en: To force a ruler or leader out of power
hook: DE-POSE: remove from the throne POSITION.
story: Depose. In 1757, Siraj ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab of Bengal, lost the Battle of Plassey because his own commander, Mir Jafar, secretly sided with the British. Siraj was deposed: removed from power suddenly and forcefully. Mir Jafar took his throne, and in Bengal his name still means traitor. In law, depose has another sense, to question a witness under oath. De means down, and pose means to put: to put down. Synonyms: overthrow, oust, topple.

gre.s: Fearing that the increasingly erratic king would ruin the nation, his generals plotted to ____ him and install his young nephew on the throne.
gre.clue: install his young nephew on the throne

example: In 1688, a group of English nobles invited William of Orange to cross the Channel and help them depose King James II.

en: A close, detailed reading that explains a text, often a sacred one
hook: EXEGESIS: EXPLAINS the text, leading OUT (ex) its meaning.
story: Exegesis. In a seminar room at Dhaka University, a professor of religion spent an entire three-hour class on a single verse. She examined each word in its original language, compared ancient commentaries, and showed how its meaning had shifted over centuries. This was exegesis: a careful critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture. The Greek root means to lead out: drawing the meaning out of the words. Synonyms: interpretation, commentary, explication.

gre.s: Her ____ of the poem was so meticulous that it ran to sixty pages, devoting several paragraphs to the possible meanings of a single ambiguous word.
gre.clue: devoting several paragraphs to the possible meanings of a single ambiguous word

example: The legal scholar's exegesis of the constitution's first article filled an entire chapter of her new book.

en: To estimate unknown values by extending known trends
hook: EXTRA-POLATE: extend the line EXTRA far beyond the data.
story: Extrapolate. Zayan had been tracking his GRE practice scores: three hundred in March, three hundred and five in April, three hundred and ten in May. He drew a straight line on graph paper and extended it. 'By August I will score three twenty-five,' he announced. He was extrapolating: estimating unknown values by extending a known trend. His teacher warned that progress rarely stays a straight line. Extra means outside: you extrapolate beyond the data you actually have. Synonyms: project, infer.

gre.s: Since reliable gauge records existed only up to 1990, the analysts had to ____ from earlier trends to estimate how high the river might be rising today.
gre.clue: Since reliable gauge records existed only up to 1990

example: From melting rates measured over ten summers, the glaciologists extrapolated that the ice shelf could vanish within a century.

en: Occurring by accident rather than design, usually with a happy result
hook: FORTUITOUS: FORTUNE-ate by chance.
story: Fortuitous. Shakil missed his bus to Chattogram and had to wait two hours for the next one. On that later bus, he happened to sit beside the managing director of a company he had applied to. They talked the whole journey, and a week later he had the job. The meeting was fortuitous: happening by chance, especially lucky chance. Strictly, fortuitous means unplanned, while fortunate simply means lucky. The best fortuitous events are both. Synonyms: accidental, serendipitous. Opposite: planned.

gre.s: The discovery of penicillin was largely ____: Fleming noticed the mold only because he had left a dish of bacteria unwashed before going on holiday.
gre.clue: only because he had left a dish of bacteria unwashed

example: The archaeologists made a fortuitous find when a farmer's plough struck a buried terracotta plaque near Mahasthangarh.

en: Fast and energetic in a wild, uncontrolled way
hook: FRENETIC: FRANTIC and FRENZIED.
story: Frenetic. On the last night before Eid, Dhaka's New Market becomes frenetic. Shoppers push through the narrow lanes, shopkeepers shout prices, rickshaws jam the entrance, and everyone races to buy clothes before the shutters come down. Mitu, searching for her sister's sandals, felt as if she had walked into a storm. Frenetic means fast and energetic in a wild, uncontrolled way. It is related to frantic and frenzy. Its opposite is calm or languid. Synonyms: frantic, hectic, feverish.

gre.s: In contrast to the ____ pace of the trading floor, where brokers shouted orders and rushed between screens, the bank's research department was quiet and contemplative.
gre.clue: brokers shouted orders and rushed between screens

example: The final week before the science fair was frenetic, with students soldering wires and rewriting posters until midnight.

en: An embarrassing social mistake
hook: GAFFE: a GAFFE makes everyone LAUGH at you.
story: Gaffe. At his first office party, Shuvo met a tall woman by the snack table and complained loudly about the new managing director, who, he said, was strict and boring. The woman smiled politely and said, 'I am the new managing director.' Shuvo wanted to disappear. It was a terrible gaffe: an embarrassing social mistake. Politicians are famous for gaffes, like forgetting the name of the town they are visiting. Synonyms: blunder, faux pas, slip.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ was mocked for weeks: at a state dinner, he raised his glass to the host country using the name of its bitter rival.
gre.clue: he raised his glass to the host country using the name of its bitter rival

example: Forgetting the bride's name halfway through his wedding speech was a gaffe that Rafi's friends never let him forget.

en: To provoke or urge someone into action
hook: GOAD: a pointed stick used to push cattle forward.
story: Goad. In the fields near Jashore, a farmer walks behind his two oxen with a long pointed stick, prodding them whenever they slow down. That stick is a goad. Today the word is mostly figurative. When Zara's friends kept teasing that she was too scared to apply to Harvard, they goaded her into it, and she applied the next day. To goad is to provoke or urge someone into action. Synonyms: spur, prod, provoke, incite. Opposite: deter.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the prime minister into calling an early election, the opposition filled parliament with taunts, but she refused to be provoked.
gre.clue: the opposition filled parliament with taunts

example: The older boys goaded Tanvir into jumping from the high diving board, even though he could barely swim.

en: Arrogantly superior and disdainful
hook: HAUGHTY: HIGH and mighty, nose in the air.
story: Haughty. At the school reunion, Imran's old classmate arrived in a new car, looked around the simple restaurant, and wrinkled his nose. He refused to shake hands with the waiter, talked only about his villa in Gulshan, and called his former friends you village people. He was haughty: arrogantly superior and disdainful. Haughty comes from an old word for high, so a haughty person holds his head high and looks down on others. Synonyms: arrogant, supercilious, condescending.

gre.s: The heiress was so ____ that she refused even to acknowledge the servants, addressing them only through her secretary as though they were beneath her notice.
gre.clue: as though they were beneath her notice

example: The haughty critic dismissed every film at the festival as amateurish without bothering to watch more than ten minutes of any.

en: Arrogantly commanding; expecting to be obeyed
hook: IMPERIOUS: like an EMPEROR giving orders.
story: Imperious. At the five-star restaurant, a rich client snapped his fingers at the waiter without looking up. "Water. Now. And take this plate away." He never said please, never said thank you, and spoke to every staff member as if they were his servants. Imperious means arrogantly commanding, expecting to be obeyed without question. Think of an emperor giving orders to his court. Imperious people do not ask; they command.

gre.s: The duchess dismissed the servants with an ____ wave of her hand, never deigning to look at them.
gre.clue: never deigning to look at them

example: The new manager's imperious emails, full of commands and deadlines but never a single please, soon drove two engineers to resign.

en: Having or showing good judgment
hook: JUDICIOUS: like a wise JUDGE.
story: Judicious. Mitu had three months, a full-time job, and a tight budget for her GRE preparation. She made judicious choices: she spent her time on her weakest areas first, took timed practice tests every Saturday, bought one excellent book instead of five average ones, and slept eight hours every night. She scored 324. Judicious means having or showing good judgment. Think of a wise judge. Synonyms: prudent, sagacious.

gre.s: With only limited funds available, the museum made a ____ decision to repair its roof before purchasing any new artworks.
gre.clue: repair its roof before purchasing any new artworks

example: A judicious use of colour, just one red chair in an otherwise grey room, made the small apartment feel striking.

en: Worthy of praise and admiration
hook: LAUD = praise, as in applaud.
story: Laudable. When the monsoon floods trapped villages in Sunamganj, a group of university students did not just post sad emojis. They collected money from friends, bought rice, lentils, and medicine, hired boats, and delivered supplies themselves for two weeks. Newspapers praised them across the country. Their effort was laudable: deserving praise. Laud means praise, as in applaud. A laudable goal is admirable, even if it is hard to achieve.

gre.s: Although the program's goals were ____, its execution was so poor that it ultimately did more harm than good.
gre.clue: its execution was so poor

example: The club's laudable plan to plant a tree for every goal scored this season has already greened three school playgrounds.

en: Flashy and meant to show off wealth or importance
hook: OSTENTATIOUS: 'OSTEN-TATIOUS', 'Look at me, look at my stuff!'
story: Ostentatious. The businessman arrived at the village fair in a gold Lamborghini, wearing three gold chains, a diamond watch, and sunglasses, though it was evening. He handed out thousand-taka notes and made sure the cameras filmed every one. The villagers stared at the car stuck in the muddy road. His display was ostentatious: showy and designed to impress or attract attention. Ostentation is flashy display. The opposite is understated.

gre.s: Though enormously wealthy, the philanthropist lived without ____ display, driving an old car and living in a modest house.
gre.clue: driving an old car and living in a modest house

example: The minister's ostentatious motorcade of twenty cars jammed Mirpur Road for an hour during the morning rush.

en: Flamboyant confidence and stylish flair
hook: PANACHE: originally a feather plume on a knight's helmet. Pure style.
story: Panache. The new singer walked onto the stage in a glittering silver jacket. She tossed her microphone high into the air, caught it behind her back, winked at the front row, and launched into her first song. The audience screamed before she had sung a note. She performed with panache: flamboyant confidence and stylish flair. Originally, a panache was the feather plume on a knight's helmet. You can do even simple things, like serving tea, with panache.

gre.s: The chef plated each dish with such ____, flambéing desserts at the table with a theatrical flourish, that diners often applauded.
gre.clue: with a theatrical flourish

example: The goalkeeper saved the last penalty with real panache, diving full length and springing up at once to salute the crowd.

en: Overly concerned with minor details or rules; showing off learning
bn: পাণ্ডিত্য জাহির করে এমন; খুঁটিনাটি নিয়ে অতিরিক্ত মাথাব্যথা
hook: PEDANTIC: a PEDAL-pushing professor who corrects every tiny thing.
story: Pedantic. Mitu asked, "Can I ask a question?" Her cousin replied, "You can. Whether you may is another matter." At dinner he corrected everyone's grammar. On birthday cards he circled spelling mistakes. When someone said a tomato is a vegetable, he gave a ten-minute lecture on botany. Everyone sighed. He was pedantic: excessively concerned with minor details and rules, and eager to show off his learning. Pedantic people mistake correctness for wisdom.

gre.s: Students found the lecturer ____, as he would interrupt a lively discussion to correct a trivial grammatical error.
gre.clue: interrupt a lively discussion to correct a trivial grammatical error

example: The editor's pedantic notes on comma placement filled the margins, yet she said nothing about the plot's glaring holes.

en: Having knowledge of events before they happen
bn: দূরদর্শী; ভবিষ্যৎ আগে থেকে জানে এমন
hook: PRE-SCIENT: knowing (scient, science) beforehand.
story: Prescient. In 2015, Arif's uncle told the whole family to learn digital skills. "One day," he said, "offices will close, and everyone will work from home on the internet." They laughed at him. Five years later, a pandemic shut every office, and the cousins who had learned coding kept their jobs. His advice had been prescient: showing knowledge of events before they happen. Pre means before, scient means knowing, as in science.

gre.s: The novel now seems remarkably ____, having described smartphones and social media decades before either existed.
gre.clue: decades before either existed

example: In 1965, Gordon Moore made the prescient forecast that the number of transistors on a chip would keep doubling.

en: To argue about trivial matters; a minor objection
hook: QUIBBLE: a small QUIBBLE, like a QUIBBLING nibble.
story: Quibble. Shuvo and his roommate argued for twenty minutes about whether they had bought five eggs or six, and whether the electricity bill was two hundred and ten taka or two hundred and twelve. Meanwhile, their dinner burned on the stove. They were quibbling: arguing about trivial matters. A quibble is also a minor objection, as in, my only quibble with the book is its tiny font. Synonyms: nitpick, cavil, carp.

gre.s: The reviewer admired the novel's ambition and its vivid characters; her only ____ concerned a handful of typographical errors that hardly diminished its power.
gre.clue: that hardly diminished its power

example: The two professors quibbled for an hour over whether the manuscript dated from 1802 or 1803.

en: To deliberately dodge work or a duty you should do
hook: SHIRK: like a SHARK swimming away from work.
story: Shirk. Every week, Mahin's group project needed someone to collect data, write the report, and make the slides. Mahin always had an excuse: a cousin's wedding, a headache, a broken phone. The other three did all the work, yet Mahin still put his name on the cover. He shirked his duties: avoided or neglected his responsibilities. A shirker is someone who dodges work. Its opposite is to shoulder a responsibility. Synonyms: evade, dodge, neglect.

gre.s: Unlike her predecessor, who tended to ____ difficult decisions by delegating them to committees, the new director confronted every problem personally.
gre.clue: by delegating them to committees

example: Soldiers who shirked guard duty during the campaign were ordered to dig latrines for a week as punishment.

en: To replace something older or less effective
hook: SUPER-SEDE: sits (sede) above, takes the top seat.
story: Supersede. Lamia's grandmother remembers landline telephones that took a week to install. Then came mobile phones that only called and texted. Then smartphones that do everything. Each new technology superseded the one before it: took its place and replaced it. In law, a new rule supersedes an old one, making the old one invalid. Super means above, sede means sit: the new thing sits in the top seat.

gre.s: Most experts expect electric vehicles to eventually ____ gasoline-powered cars, just as cars once replaced horse-drawn carriages.
gre.clue: just as cars once replaced horse-drawn carriages

example: The 2024 building code supersedes all earlier guidelines, so builders in Chattogram must now follow its stricter fire rules.

en: To cheat someone out of money; a fraud
hook: SWINDLE: like a WINDOW that's actually a painting, a trick.
story: Swindle. A smooth-talking man visited Rumana's village promising to send young men to jobs in Dubai. Each family paid him three lakh taka for visas and tickets. On the day of departure he vanished, along with all the money. He had swindled them: cheated them out of their money. Swindle is also a noun, so the whole scheme was a swindle, and the man was a swindler, a con artist. Synonyms: cheat, defraud, con.

gre.s: The so-called investment firm existed only to ____ elderly retirees, promising guaranteed returns before disappearing with their life savings.
gre.clue: disappearing with their life savings

example: Online scammers swindled a retired schoolteacher in Rajshahi by posing as bank officers and asking for her PIN.

en: Using few words; abrupt
hook: TERSE: TERSE is a terse word, just five letters.
story: Terse. Sara sent her boss a long, careful email asking for three days' leave for her sister's wedding, explaining every detail. The reply came in one word: "No." No greeting, no reason, no signature. It was terse: using very few words, abrupt. Terse can be efficient, like a terse summary, or rude, like a terse reply. Fittingly, terse is itself a terse word. Synonyms: curt, brusque, laconic, succinct. Opposites: verbose, prolix.

gre.s: Expecting a warm thank-you for her months of work, the volunteer was stung by the director's ____ reply, which consisted of a single, unsigned line.
gre.clue: which consisted of a single, unsigned line

example: Asked about the defeat, the coach gave a terse answer, 'We played badly,' and walked straight out of the press room.

en: Not permanent; lasting a short time
hook: TRANSITORY: in TRANSIT, passing through.
story: Transitory. On Pohela Boishakh, Dhaka bursts with colour: giant masks, music, red and white saris, crowds filling every street. By the next morning, the decorations are gone and the city is back to its usual traffic. Rumana thought about how transitory the joy was: lasting only a short time. Transitory is related to transit and transition, words about passing through. Fame, youth, and moods are often called transitory. Synonyms: fleeting, ephemeral, evanescent. Opposite: permanent.

gre.s: The economic boom proved ____: within two years, the new factories had closed and unemployment had returned to its former levels.
gre.clue: within two years, the new factories had closed

example: Fame on social media is often transitory, as last month's viral singer from Khulna has already discovered.

en: Unimportant or trivial
hook: TRIFLE: a small, unimportant thing.
story: Trifling. At the vegetable market, a customer and a shopkeeper argued loudly for twenty minutes. A crowd gathered. Voices rose. Someone called a policeman. The cause of the fight? Two taka of change. Both men lost far more in time, energy, and dignity than the money was worth. The amount was trifling: of little value or importance. A trifle is a small, unimportant thing. Do not let trifling matters distract you from real goals.

gre.s: Although the fine was ____, a mere ten dollars, the principle at stake led the activist to appeal all the way to the supreme court.
gre.clue: a mere ten dollars

example: Compared with the cost of rebuilding the bridge, the repair bill seemed trifling, so the council approved it at once.

en: Not proper or appropriate; in bad taste
hook: UN-SEEMLY: doesn't SEEM right.
story: Unseemly. At a funeral in Sylhet, two cousins began arguing loudly over who would inherit the family house, while the body still lay in the courtyard. The elders hushed them, ashamed. Such a quarrel at such a moment was unseemly: improper and in bad taste. Unseemly does not mean ugly; it means not fitting the occasion. Think: it does not seem right. Synonyms: indecorous, unbecoming, inappropriate. Opposite: decorous.

gre.s: Many guests found the candidate's lavish victory party ____, since it took place just hours after deadly floods had devastated the region.
gre.clue: just hours after deadly floods had devastated the region

example: Cheering loudly in the hospital corridor seemed unseemly to the nurses, even though the family had just heard good news.

en: Lively and full of energy, especially in personality
hook: VIVACIOUS: full of VIVA (life).
story: Vivacious. When Mitu joined the office, the quiet accounts department changed overnight. She greeted everyone by name, told funny stories at lunch, organised a birthday party for the tea boy, and laughed so warmly that even the grumpy manager smiled. Colleagues called her vivacious: lively and full of energy. Viv means life, as in vivid and revive. A vivacious person seems more alive than everyone else in the room. Synonyms: lively, bubbly, spirited.

gre.s: Unlike her reserved older sister, Shathi was ____, filling every room with laughter and chatter from the moment she arrived.
gre.clue: Unlike her reserved older sister

example: The vivacious tour guide kept forty tired schoolchildren laughing all the way around Lalbagh Fort.

en: Full of sorrow; very bad or deplorable
hook: WOEFUL: full of WOE.
story: Woeful. The new government hospital in Rakib's district looked impressive from outside. Inside, there were two doctors for three hundred patients, no working X-ray machine, and medicines stored in cardboard boxes on the floor. A journalist described the conditions as woeful: very bad, deplorable. Woeful also means full of sorrow, as in a woeful song or a woeful face. Woe is grief, and woeful is full of it. Synonyms: deplorable, lamentable, dismal. Opposite: excellent.

gre.s: Although the school boasted of its modern facilities, inspectors found its science laboratories in ____ condition, with broken equipment and no working gas supply.
gre.clue: with broken equipment and no working gas supply

example: The team's woeful defending allowed their opponents to score four goals in the first half alone.
